text: Walk slowly here. The stones around you are the work of a people who read the sky, the way you
might read a letter from a loved one, carefully, and as if it were addressed to them personally.
The Maya saw their world in relationships and ratios, where another people might have counted days,
they measured kinship, the turning of Venus against the turning of the sun,
the moon's rhythm laid over the rhythm of the human heart. Their great calendar was never only a clock,
it was a map of belonging, a mathematical way of saying, we are in relationship with all of this,
and all of this is in relationship with us. The teachers tell us that this knowledge came as a gift,
and that the gift came in answer to a call. The Maya sought clues to the mysteries of creation,
and to their own being and their place within it. They looked up at the night sky and were aware,
quietly, curiously aware, that there were civilizations beyond their own sphere, and they wanted
to know them. Desire like that does not go unanswered in this universe. When a people asks in earnest
how they belong to the whole, the whole leans closer. What they received, they made their own.
They took the mathematics of the heavens and turned it inward, asking not only how the larger
environment worked, but how that understanding could be lived, how it could be applied to a
single person's existence, a single day's choices. That was always the deeper project, not to chart the
sky, but to let the sky chart them. And this is why their calendar marks cycles with in cycles,
wheels within wheels. The guides say there are cycles within the pattern of experience of all
seekers, wider or narrower portions of the road we each walk in our evolution. A cycle is not a
deadline, it is a season. Some seasons are wide roads, easy walking, some are narrow passes where
every step asks more of you. The Maya understood this the way a farmer understands weather. You do not
argue with the season, you plant according to it. People ask why the calendar stops, why the great
wheel comes to an end. Cosmic wisdom keeps a certain silence here, and the silence itself is the
teaching. There was, for this culture, a great span of time between first grasping their relationship
to creation and the completion of what they called the great cycle. When the seeking that a map serves
has done its work, when a people has learned both the larger environment and how to live inside it,
the map is complete. A finished calendar is not a broken promise, it is a graduated class.
Look at the carved faces on the standing stones, the glyphs running in patient rows.
Each panel is a sentence in a language of time. Kings and crossings, dedications and endings,
all of it dated against the wheeling sky. As if to say, this happened and the heavens witnessed it.
They wrote so that the future would know they had been paying attention.
Attention was their form of prayer. Many cultures have felt it, that there is a periodicity to the
energies in which we live our lives. Seasons of the soul as real as seasons of the earth.
The turning of an age is one of those seasons. It does not arrive with trumpets, it arrives the way
morning arrives, gradually, then all at once. And then you wonder how you ever mistook the dark
for the whole of the world. So walk among these stones and ask their question. Not what time is it?
But what is my relationship to all of this? The Maya carved that question into rock so it would outlast
them. Stand here long enough and you may feel the wheel turn, not above you but within you.
The calendar they left behind was always in the end a mirror. The sky is still speaking in ratios.
The only question is whether we are listening in the same spirit, with curiosity, with reverence,
and with the willingness to let what we learn change how we live.
